Divorced
di-vorst'
v. and a. (put away from a marriage; regulated for the priesthood, for vows, and addressed directly by our Lord in the Sermon on the Mount)
From Latin divortium, a separation, from divertere, to turn aside. The Hebrew at Leviticus 21:14 is gerushah, a woman driven out, from garash, to expel; the Greek at Matthew 5:32 is apoluo, to release or put away.

Biblical Definition

The Mosaic law did not institute divorce; it regulated a practice already in existence and restricted its consequences. A priest might not marry a divorced woman: “A widow, or a divorced woman, or profane, or an harlot, these shall he not take: but he shall take a virgin of his own people to wife” (Leviticus 21:14), the high priest being held to a stricter standard than the congregation. A divorced woman's vows stood on her own head rather than a husband's or father's: “every vow of a widow, and of her that is divorced, wherewith they have bound their souls, shall stand against her” (Numbers 30:9) — a provision that recognises her as a legal person in her own right. Our Lord addresses the matter directly: “whosoever shall put away his wife, saving for the cause of fornication, causeth her to commit adultery: and whosoever shall marry her that is divorced committeth adultery” (Matthew 5:32). When pressed on Deuteronomy 24 He went behind Moses to the creation ordinance: they are no more twain but one flesh, “What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder” (Matthew 19:6) — and said Moses suffered it for the hardness of their hearts, but from the beginning it was not so.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines divorce as a legal dissolution of the bond of matrimony, and notes the distinction between total dissolution and separation from bed and board.

expand to see more

DIVORCED, pp. Separated from a husband or wife by law; parted.

DIVORCE, n. A legal dissolution of the bonds of matrimony, or the separation of husband and wife by a judicial sentence.

2. The separation of a married woman from the bed and board of her husband.

3. Separation; disunion of things closely united.

DIVORCE, v.t. To dissolve the marriage contract, and thus to separate husband and wife.

Key Scripture

Matthew 19:6 — "Wherefore they are no more twain, but one flesh. What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder."

Matthew 5:32 — "But I say unto you, That whosoever shall put away his wife, saving for the cause of fornication, causeth her to commit adultery: and whosoever shall marry her that is divorced committeth adultery."

Leviticus 21:14 — "A widow, or a divorced woman, or profane, or an harlot, these shall he not take: but he shall take a virgin of his own people to wife."

Numbers 30:9 — "But every vow of a widow, and of her that is divorced, wherewith they have bound their souls, shall stand against her."

Modern Corruption

No-fault divorce has made marriage terminable at will, and the church has largely followed the culture into treating it as a private and reversible arrangement.

expand to see more

The legal revolution of the last sixty years replaced fault-based divorce with dissolution on demand, and the practical result is that marriage is now the only contract in Western law that either party may void unilaterally without cause. Our Lord's teaching runs directly against it. Asked which grounds were sufficient — the standing rabbinic debate — He declined to argue about grounds and went to the creation ordinance: God made them male and female, a man shall leave father and mother and cleave to his wife, and they two shall be one flesh. What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder assumes a joining that man did not perform and therefore cannot dissolve at pleasure.

Scripture is not silent about the exceptions, and pastoral honesty requires naming them: our Lord excepts fornication, and Paul in 1 Corinthians 7 addresses the departure of an unbelieving spouse. The confessional Reformed position has held those two grounds and refused to multiply them. What the tradition has also insisted on, and what is most often neglected, is the direction of Christ's concern in Matthew 5:32 — He speaks of what a man's putting away does to her. In a society where a discarded wife had almost no means of support, the sin He names is the injury done by the stronger party to the weaker, and that emphasis should govern how the church handles these cases still.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew gerushah, a woman driven out — Leviticus 21:14; garash, to expel; kerithuth, a cutting off, a bill of divorcement — Deuteronomy 24:1; Greek apoluo, to release — Matthew 5:32.

expand to see more

Hebrew gerushah — a woman put away; Leviticus 21:14 and Numbers 30:9.

Hebrew garash — to drive out, expel; the root of the noun.

Hebrew sepher kerithuth — a bill of cutting off; the writing of Deuteronomy 24:1.

Greek apoluo — to loose from, release, put away; Matthew 5:32 and 19:3.

Greek chorizo — to separate; Matthew 19:6, “let not man put asunder.”

Usage

"“What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder” — the creation ordinance."

"“From the beginning it was not so” — our Lord going behind Moses to Genesis."

"“Every vow… shall stand against her” — the divorced woman as a legal person."
